title: TIP: paclitaxel, ifosfamide and cisplatin
purpose: Treat relapsed or resistant testicular germ-cell cancer, with the possibility of lasting remission in selected patients.
schedule_label: Chemotherapy days 1–5 · every 21 days · four cycles
schedule_summary: Paclitaxel is given on day 1. Cisplatin and ifosfamide are given on days 1–5, with bladder-protecting mesna each day. Growth-factor injections start on day 6 until neutrophil recovery under local policy. Four 21-day cycles are planned, subject to consultant review.
administration_text: Paclitaxel runs over three hours on day 1, cisplatin over one hour and ifosfamide over two hours on days 1–5. Mesna is given immediately before ifosfamide and again four and eight hours after the ifosfamide infusion finishes. The unit coordinates the complete schedule; do not calculate home timings yourself.
monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney and liver profile before each treatment. Staff check neurological function daily during ifosfamide and urine for blood before and daily during it. Review hearing, nerves, hydration, electrolytes and fluid balance.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
risks: Hair loss, muscle or joint pain
Mouth, bowel, skin and nail effects

agents.name: Ifosfamide
agents.mechanism: Damages DNA needed for cell division
agents.explanation: Ifosfamide damages cancer-cell DNA. Its breakdown products can also affect the bladder, kidneys and brain. Mesna protects the bladder but does not prevent all kidney or brain effects.
risks: Low blood counts, serious infection, anaemia and bleeding
Bladder inflammation and bleeding; kidney and electrolyte problems
Nausea, mouth soreness, hair loss, fatigue and fertility harm
Rare serious heart or lung effects and later blood cancers
agents.watch: Report confusion, sleepiness, blood in urine or reduced urine immediately.

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
agents.watch: Report ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which can persist
Numbness or tingling, which can persist
Electrolyte changes and need for hydration

rows.label: Medicines and practical care
cells: Confirm the five-day attendance/admission plan, mesna timings, hydration, allergy prevention and growth-factor prescription.

Paclitaxel runs over three hours on day 1, cisplatin over one hour and ifosfamide over two hours on days 1–5. Mesna is given immediately before ifosfamide and again four and eight hours after the ifosfamide infusion finishes. The unit coordinates the complete schedule; do not calculate home timings yourself.

Cisplatin needs a high-risk anti-sickness plan and prescribed hydration/electrolytes. Ifosfamide needs mesna and adequate fluids. Paclitaxel needs prescribed allergy premedication; reconcile steroid doses with antiemetics. Aprepitant may increase ifosfamide brain toxicity, so pharmacy must review the combination. Growth factor is included from day 6. Retain prescribed mouth care, pain relief and stomach protection.
Review lasting effects, support needs and any line/pump removal.

evidence.title: MRC phase II TIP study · Mead2005
evidence.summary: Among 43 patients eligible for response assessment, the favourable response rate was 60% (95% confidence interval44–75%). This combined complete responses with partial responses in which tumour markers became negative.
evidence.intro: Among 43 patients eligible for response assessment, the favourable response rate was 60% (95% confidence interval44–75%). This combined complete responses with partial responses in which tumour markers became negative.
evidence.caveat: This small, non-randomised study used ifosfamide1000 mg/m²/day, compared with 1200 mg/m²/day in NCCP 00602. A favourable response is not the same as cure, and these results cannot predict an individual outcome.
evidence.interpretation: This small, non-randomised study used ifosfamide1000 mg/m²/day, compared with 1200 mg/m²/day in NCCP 00602. A favourable response is not the same as cure, and these results cannot predict an individual outcome.

questions.a: Treat relapsed or resistant testicular germ-cell cancer, with the possibility of lasting remission in selected patients. The germ-cell specialist team chooses salvage chemotherapy using previous response, relapse timing, tumour markers and disease extent. Surgery for remaining masses or a high-dose stem-cell pathway may be considered separately; neither is automatically part of this calendar.

questions.q: Does a delay mean treatment has failed?
questions.a: No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.

questions.q: Who do I contact if unwell?
questions.a: Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.
